Research

Social Capital & Life Satisfaction

City St George's, University of London | 2024 | Dissertation mark: 71%

  • Modelled the link between social capital and life satisfaction across five countries in R, using the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) 2017 module (n = 11,249) as one instrument for all three of Putnam's dimensions.
  • Methods: multiple imputation (MICE), PCA-built constructs, country-level and pooled OLS with interaction terms, Tukey pairwise comparisons, and AIC/BIC model comparison.
  • Perceived institutional fairness was the most consistent cross-cultural predictor of life satisfaction. Relative income (within-country brackets) had no significant main effect, but as income rose, the links between life satisfaction and trust, daily contact and organisational contact weakened.
  • Social capital mattered more where state capacity was weaker (lower human development, fewer government resources, more corruption), while better governance had its own positive effect on life satisfaction.
  • Made policy recommendations on institutional transparency, civic infrastructure and bridging social capital.
